query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exhibiting native surface defects and inhomogeneities verified by high-resolution TEM and XPS analysis.
generation.intervention: Subject nanoparticles to controlled laser heating with in situ TEM observation while comparing two sets: one with standard (defect-rich) surfaces and another with chemically passivated surfaces (with minimized defects using gentle surface treatments confirmed by XPS).
generation.conditions: Rapid heating in the premelting temperature regime under identical thermal ramp rates in an inert or vacuum environment to prevent oxidation; surface chemical state characterized pre- and post-treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface defect sites and atomic-scale roughness that serve as nucleation sites for local melting, with passivated surfaces exhibiting fewer active sites.
generation.mechanism: Local atomic rearrangements preferentially occur at defect sites, where the energy barrier to melting is reduced. These sites become initial nucleation centers for a liquid-like surface layer, which propagates inward. Quantitatively, nanoparticles with high defect densities are predicted to show a decrease in the apparent melting onset temperature by 10–15% compared to passivated samples.
generation.predicted_outcome: Defect-rich nanoparticles will display earlier onset of surface melting (by approximately 10–15% lower temperature) and reveal liquid-like surface layers via in situ TEM, whereas passivated nanoparticles will show delayed and more uniform melting.
generation.baseline: Untreated nanoparticles with intrinsic defect densities that exhibit conventional premelting behavior without pronounced early surface melting.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is valid for nanoparticle sizes and defect densities typical of solid-phase synthesis; if nanoparticles are extremely small or possess unusually thick oxide layers, the behavior may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Although a reduction in melting onset by roughly 10–15% is predicted, the precise value and spatial extent of the liquid region depend on defect density and may require further calibration through simulation and experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one with standard defect density and one with surfaces chemically passivated (confirmed by XPS). Use controlled laser heating with in situ TEM to observe the onset of surface melting and compare the onset temperatures.
measurements: Melting onset temperature differences via in situ TEM
Spatial mapping of liquid-like surface regions
Surface chemical state via pre- and post-heating XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no distinguishable 10–15% reduction in the melting onset temperature or if both passivated and untreated particles show similar surface melting behavior, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As described above, during laser irradiation, the conversion of the HEA NPs from the mixed metal precursors adsorbed on LIG involves several processes, including thermal decomposition, metal ion reduction, metallic element melting, molten bead fusion, and fission, depending on the temperature experience. The laser synthesis in this work is based on solid-phase, which is different from liquid-phase synthesis. As the mixed metal precursor is adsorbed on the 3D porous LIG structure and dried before laser irradiation, the size of the nanoparticles can be well controlled by the laser fluence, and the concentration of the precursor due to the limited mobility of the reduced metal species and subsequently the nanoparticles.

Our work provides direct visualization of nanoparticles on amorphous carbon supports and elucidate the details of amorphous carbon graphitization during ultrafast exposure to extremely high temperatures under electrical Joule heating process. The in situ TEM studies of Joule heating on amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors show that during the Joule heating process, the CNFs undergo volumetric expansion due to amorphous to crystalline phase transition, which is also associated with formation and stabilization of metallic nanoparticles on the carbon supports. The crystallized CNFs are made of T-graphite with a high density of randomly dispersed edge planes. These edge planes are highly defective and act as preferred sites for the nucleation of metallic nanoparticles. In addition, metal atoms diffuse into layered structure strengthening the anchoring of the nanoparticles on the edge planes. This prevents the nanoparticles from further aggregation at extremely high temperatures as confirmed by MD simulation and in situ heating in TEM. In this work, while Pt nanoparticles are described as a model synthesis system, the same observation is made for Ru and multicomponent Pd
